A call glyph pulses beneath the notice. *Ressa Morn.*

“I can call her,” Ivo says. “If it’s her book, she’ll answer. If it isn’t—”

“If it isn’t,” the hooded figure says, “you will tell whoever is holding it where to find the people you have been trying to save.”

Ivo turns on them. “You know nothing about them.”

“I know you sold Calyx’s name to make a debt smaller.”

The rain seems to narrow around that sentence. Ivo’s face has gone pale under the lane-light, but there is anger in it now too—real anger, not the borrowed kind that makes a man feel less ashamed of himself.

The figure lowers the pouch. “Six minutes. Ora Pell for the custody half. Or take the pouch and make your own record of what you think you saw. It is already tagged to this bay. You will not be the first person tonight to discover that possession and proof are different problems.”

They set it back on the dolly.

There is no threat of a weapon. No raised voice. Only a piece of paper in the rain, Ivo’s family on a countdown, and the sharp knowledge that Niko and Ora are moving through a route somebody may now try to price.

The hooded figure waits beyond the lamp’s circle. Ivo’s thumb hovers over Ressa Morn’s call glyph, unable to press it alone.

What do you spend first?

Make Ivo call Ressa Morn on speaker and force the debt-book threat into a witnessed conversation before the lane closes.

You pull a memorial slate from beneath the lantern rack: black polymer, old enough that its surface has been scored and sanded by hands who preferred their dead and their grievances to outlast a server lease. Calyx clears a space beside the first page. The rain makes a private weather of the hall, softening every breath beyond the chamber.

“Not an explanation,” you say. “An account.”

Elian looks at you for a long moment. Her hand is still closed around the brass key, its teeth pressed into the heel of her palm.

“Write what it says,” she tells Calyx. “Write what it does not say too.”

Calyx nods once and sets pencil to slate-paper.

She begins with the conditions of its survival: the transfer order recovered from the severed Quill relay; the chain beyond its first page made legally uncertifiable by the severance; the page itself directly observed by those in the chamber. Then she reads the authorization aloud, word by word, refusing the bureaucratic cadence the mercy of smoothness.

“Dr. Sera Vey,” she says, “authorizes emergency mortuary transfer of Elian Rook. Rationale: unreconciled proximity to Mara Vey’s pre-collapse variance; direct reconciliation contraindicated.”

Your mother’s name crosses the room and becomes something material there.

Calyx waits.

Elian’s face has gone still in the way a station window goes still when the storm beyond it has become too large to look at. When she speaks, her voice is low and exact.

“Add this: the order names Mara Vey as a condition. It does not establish that Mara knew the order existed. It does not establish what Dr. Vey intended by it. It does not establish that I consented. It does not establish that I was safe.”

The pencil moves.

“And,” Elian says, looking not at the page but at you, “it does not make her mother’s reasons into my story.”

“No,” you say.

It is all you have any right to say. It is enough to make the word costly.

Vela steps nearer, but stops short of the slate. “The phrase *direct reconciliation contraindicated* was used for a narrow category of cases,” she says. “Children whose records had become entangled with an adult continuity risk. It meant the Office believed an edit to one life might destabilize another.”

Elian turns her head.

“Believed?”

Vela’s mouth tightens. “Claimed. Sometimes believed. The corridor made a habit of treating the difference as administrative.”

Calyx writes that too, under a separate heading: *Vela Nash’s contextual statement; not verified by the recovered order.* She looks to Elian before she commits it. Elian gives the smallest nod.

Ren remains outside the relay threshold, as he has promised. The amber wafer in his palm pulses once more, then changes.

Green light spills across his fingers.

For an instant no one speaks. The external mirror has accepted the blind audit: 49-Delta revoked; unlawful extension entered; Ren Vale’s name attached to both the wound and the attempt to close it.

Ren exhales through his nose. Not relief. Something more like the moment a person realizes the bridge behind them has actually burned.

“The mirror is live,” he says. “Any use of that reference now will carry my revocation with it.”

“Good,” Elian says. “Let it carry the rest of us too.”

Calyx tears the slate-paper free, then makes two copies with the hall’s carbon press. The first remains beside the relay glass, signed by Calyx and countersigned by three mourners who heard every qualification. The second she folds into Elian’s keeping without touching the brass key. The third she holds over the little votive flame near the memorial rack—not close enough to burn, only close enough for the rain-warped ink to dry in public view.

Tam Oris watches all of it with the terrible concentration of someone learning how quickly a name can become a route. At last they say, “If Morrow’s people see that wording, they’ll know the old corridor is exposed. They may strip the registrar stacks before we get there.”

Beyond the loading arcade, freight metal groans. A new sound follows it: three tones, a pause, then three more—Niko’s dockside cadence, faint through the rain.

This time there is no answer.

The account is durable now, though not invulnerable. It says exactly what Sera Vey’s signature can bear and refuses every comfort somebody might try to build on top of it. But the corridor may be closing, Tam’s name is in the record, and somewhere in the coolant lanes the third receipt has gone quiet.

What do you move to save next?

Go after the silence in the coolant lanes and find out what has happened to Niko and Calyx’s third receipt.

Niko does not hesitate.

He braces one boot against the wall, catches the torn terminal housing by its loose lower lip, and drives his elbow into the exposed relay nest.

The screen goes white.

For one thin second, the unfinished header fills with a spill of antique registrar glyphs—then the display folds inward on itself with a dry electrical crack. The ash-gray seal gutters out. Somewhere above the bay, a lock releases with a sound like a breath being taken back.

The shutter lever jumps beneath Niko’s hand.

“Pinned signal’s gone,” he says. “Doesn’t mean they’ve gone.”

The coolant pumps swallow the silence after it. Without the terminal’s pale light, the worklamp makes islands of all your faces: Ora’s weathered and immovable; Niko’s sharpened toward the half-open shutter; Ivo’s suddenly stripped of the one thing he had been using as a shield—the idea that there might still be a deal to make.

You step toward him.

“Who holds your debt?”

Ivo looks past you at the dead terminal, as if it might answer in his place.

“Ressa Morn,” he says at last.

Ora’s mouth hardens.

“Of course it is,” she says.

Ivo’s eyes cut toward her. “She holds the contracts. The favors. The names of who guaranteed whom when the docks went lean. Mine started as freight money. Then it became the kind of debt where somebody’s sister loses a berth if you miss a payment.” His voice catches, and he forces it level. “Ressa keeps the book. She doesn’t forgive. She restructures.”

“And the settlement offer?” you ask.

“I never heard her voice.”

“Then why believe it?”

“Because it came through a debt chime only she can authorize.” He digs two fingers into the inner seam of his raincoat and brings out a cheap, water-sealed receiver. Its casing is scored with old handling. “It knew the first name of the woman who co-signed for me. It knew the berth number of my brother’s kid. Things aren’t supposed to know those unless they have Ressa’s book—or Ressa.”

Niko watches Ivo’s hands, not his face. “What did you give them?”

The question lands cleanly. Ivo does not evade it.

“Not the route.”

Ora makes a contemptuous sound.

“I gave them Calyx’s name two weeks ago,” Ivo says. “I thought they wanted a witness they could frighten into quiet. I thought I could sell them a name and keep the rest.” He looks at you then, and there is no appeal in it. Only the shape of his own failure. “They knew Ora before I came here. That part is mine.”

Rainwater ticks from the pipes. In the memorial hall, somewhere beyond the maze of metal and concrete, Elian is keeping an account alive that Ivo helped place in danger.

Ora rises from the crate. The biscuit tin remains chained behind her.

“You brought a price to my door,” she says. “Now you tell us whether Ressa sold you, or whether somebody reached into her book and started wearing her hands.”

“I don’t know,” Ivo says.

It might be true. It is not enough.

From beyond the shutter comes three soft impacts against the metal.

Not Niko’s cadence. Not a maintenance knock.

A pause.

Then one more.

Niko’s hand closes around the emergency lever. “They know the terminal went dark,” he says. “And they know we chose not to take their window.”

Ivo stares at the receiver in his palm. “If I call Ressa, she’ll either tell me who used her chime”—he swallows—“or she’ll know I’m against the settlement.”

Ora reaches beneath the crate and draws out a long-handled cutting bar, old-fashioned enough to have a wooden grip. She does not raise it. She merely holds it where everyone can see what sort of woman has kept a paper route alive this long.

The dead terminal has bought you privacy, not safety. Outside, whoever came for the route has stopped pretending to be a system.

What do you spend first?

Have Niko force the shutter and move Ora before the people outside can choose the ground for you.

Niko does not ask Ora twice.

He drops the emergency lever with both hands.

The shutter rises hard enough to shake rust from its track. Rain-silvered air knifes into the bay, carrying the iron smell of the canal channels and the far-off sweetness of somebody’s tea stall burning cheap sugar. Beyond the threshold, the service lane lies empty for exactly the length of a held breath.

Then a freight dolly rolls out of the dark.

Not fast. Not trying to strike anyone. Its little wheels tick over the grating with an almost domestic patience. A municipal maintenance lamp has been magnet-clamped to its handle, throwing white light across a sealed waterproof pouch and a narrow strip of paper taped to the dolly’s deck.

**ONE HALF FOR ONE NAME.**

Ora sees the pouch and goes still in a manner more dangerous than fear.

“They found a piece,” she says.

“Maybe,” Ivo says.

“Maybe you shut your mouth.”

Niko is already moving. He catches Ora by the elbow—not rough, but absolute—and takes her sideways, away from the line of the shutter. You catch the chained biscuit tin as she lets it go, its weight thudding into your palm. Old metal. Old locks. A small, stubborn gravity.

“West conduit,” Niko says. “Two turns, then the lift cage. We can lose the lane cameras in the condensers.”

Ora digs her heel in. “The other half is not on me.”

“I know,” he says. “That’s why you have to leave alive enough to know where it is tomorrow.”

A sound comes from the opposite end of the service lane: a door unclenching on its seal.

No footsteps follow it.

That is worse.

Niko pushes the shutter just high enough for the bay to become a mouth, not a firing line. He takes position at its edge, scanning the rain-dark geometry beyond. The cutting bar in Ora’s hand looks suddenly ceremonial beside him—an oath from a slower, more honest kind of violence.

Ivo’s receiver wakes.

A single chime, bright and intimate in the pump-noise.

His face drains. He does not touch it.

The display shows no caller. Only a line of dock-contract code, and beneath it, a sentence in plain text:

**THE BOY’S GUARANTOR HAS MISSED TWO SHIFTS. CALL BACK BEFORE THE LANE CLOSES.**

Ivo folds over the receiver as if he has been struck.

“They’re using Ressa’s book,” he says. “Or she is.”

Another movement at the far end of the lane: the vague silhouette of a person beneath a maintenance hood, stationary behind the dolly’s light. They make no move to enter. They do not need to. The pouch waits in the rain between you, offering a fragment of Calyx’s record in exchange for the person who knows how the fragments were divided.

Ora’s eyes find yours. The anger in them has not diminished. It has become calculation.

“Move me,” she says. “But don’t let them make my route into a rescue story. They are not here for me alone.”

Behind you, the hall’s thick walls keep Elian, Tam, Calyx, Ren, and the newly durable account beyond easy reach. Ahead, the west conduit is narrow, wet, and unmonitored only because it was never meant to carry people. Niko can get Ora moving now—but the dolly, the pouch, and Ivo’s threatened family will remain in the lane for someone else to own.

The figure under the hood lifts one hand and taps the sealed pouch once.

A counteroffer. Or bait.

What do you carry out of this threshold?

Send Niko with Ora while you stay in the bay to confront the hooded figure and learn what half of the receipt they claim to hold.

Elian does not try to stop you. She catches your wrist once—not to hold you, only to make sure you meet her eyes.

“Bring him back if you can,” she says.

It is not an order to save the paper over the person, or the person over the paper. She has learned too much tonight about what those false choices cost.

“I’ll keep this account breathing,” Calyx says, already turning toward the hall and its witnesses.

Ren’s gaze follows you to the loading arcade. “My people can—”

“No,” you say.

The word comes quicker than your exhaustion. His officers would turn a search into a jurisdiction. Whatever has happened in the coolant lanes, it has already had enough of those.

Vela points through the rain-curtain beyond the freight lifts. “Lower return channel. Past the condenser stacks. There’s an old shutter with a saint scratched into it.”

Niko’s cadence does not sound again.

You go.

The arcade gives way to maintenance dark: ribbed metal underfoot, pipes sweating warm water overhead, the station’s hidden bloodstream rushing behind thin walls. Rain from the weather lattice has found its way down through every bad seam. It drips from cable trays in slow, bright beads. Your shoes splash through runoff carrying rust, machine oil, and a pale thread of incense from the memorial hall.

At the third turn, you find the saint.

Someone has scratched a small lantern into the shutter and given it a crooked halo.

It is half-closed.

Inside the narrow service bay, Ora Pell sits on an overturned crate beneath a hanging worklight. She is older than the hall’s mourners, wrapped in a dockcoat patched so many times it has become a map of other people’s hands. One palm rests on a biscuit tin chained to the crate beside her.

Niko stands between her and the opening, wet to the shoulders, one hand braced against the shutter’s emergency lever. He is breathing hard but upright.

Across from him is Ivo Senn.

No weapon. No theatrical threat. Just Ivo in a black raincoat, with both hands visible and fear working visibly beneath his calculation. A service terminal on the wall has been torn open; its small screen shivers with static.

For a second, all three of them look at you as though your arrival has changed the terms. It has not. Not yet.

“I found him,” Niko says. “He found Ora first.”

Ora gives a dry, humorless click of her tongue. “Found my outer door. He never found my paper.”

Ivo’s eyes flick to the chained tin, then away too quickly.

“The third receipt is not in there,” he says.

“Then why are you still staring at it?” Ora asks.

The terminal clears.

A municipal seal blooms on its cracked display—not Continuity blue, but the antique ash-gray used in the old registrar systems. Beneath it, a single line types itself out.

**PRIORITY: ASH. SETTLEMENT OFFER REMAINS OPEN.**

Then another.

**SENN: DELIVER THE WITNESS ROUTE. PELL: DELIVER THE DERIVATIVE.**

No name signs it. No threat is spoken. The threat is in the fact that it knows exactly who is standing in this room.

Ivo flinches as if the screen has struck him.

“They offered to clear my debt,” he says. His voice is low, almost lost under the coolant pumps. “Not just the money. The people holding it. They said they’d unmake the whole chain if I gave them Calyx’s route.”

Niko does not lower his hand from the shutter lever. “And?”

Ivo looks at you, not at Niko.

“And I came here before they did.”

It could be the beginning of an apology. It could be the first move in a better sale.

Ora’s fingers tighten on the tin’s chain. “I split the third sheet,” she says. “Not copied. Split. One half went out with a line-rat before your boy’s chirp died. The other half is somewhere no municipal screen can ask after.”

Niko’s expression changes by a fraction: relief, immediately disciplined.

“The shutter’s been remotely pinned,” he says. “I can force it up, but whoever owns that terminal will know which way we run. Or we can kill the terminal and stay blind in here.”

On the display, a third line begins to form. The cursor blinks after a routing header:

**EARLY CONTINUITY CUSTODIAL REVIEW — LIVE TRANSFER WINDOW:**

It has not yet supplied the destination.

Ivo sees it and goes pale.

“They weren’t buying paper,” he says. “They were buying the route to whoever carried it.”

The coolant lane hums around the four of you. Behind you, the memorial hall holds Elian’s account against the rain. Ahead, a system that should be dead is preparing to tell you where it still has a door.

What do you move first?

Have Niko kill the terminal while you press Ivo to explain exactly who holds his debt and what he knows about the settlement offer.
